[[File:Karlsruhe Bodenehr 1721 koloriert.jpg|thumb|View of Karlsruhe in 1721]]
In [[metric geometry]], the '''Karlsruhe metric''' is a [[metric space|measure of distance]] that assumes travel is only possible along rays through the [[origin (mathematics)|origin]] and circular arcs centered at the origin. The name alludes to the layout of the city of [[Karlsruhe]], which has radial streets and circular avenues around a central point. This metric is also called '''Moscow metric'''.<ref>[http://www.personal.kent.edu/~rmuhamma/Compgeometry/MyCG/CG-Applets/VoroKarlsruhe/karlcli.htm Karlsruhe-Metric Voronoi Diagram]</ref><ref>{{cite conference |last1=Klein |first1=Rolf |title=Abstract Voronoi diagrams and their applications |book-title=Computational Geometry and its Applications |date=1988 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |pages=148–157 |doi=10.1007/3-540-50335-8_31}}</ref>

In this metric, there are two types of shortest paths. One possibility, when the two points are on nearby rays, combines a circular arc through the nearer to the origin of the two points and a segment of a ray through the farther of the two points. Alternatively, for points on rays that are nearly opposite, it is shorter to follow one ray all the way to the origin and then follow the other ray back out. Therefore, the Karlsruhe distance between two points <math>d_k(p_1,p_2)</math> is the minimum of the two lengths that would be obtained for these two types of path. That is, it equals
<math display=block>
d_k(p_1,p_2)= \begin{cases}
\min(r_1,r_2) \cdot \delta(p_1,p_2) +|r_1-r_2|,&\text{if } 0\leq \delta(p_1,p_2)\leq 2\\
r_1+r_2,&\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
</math>
where <math>(r_i,\varphi_i)</math> are the [[Polar coordinate system|polar coordinates]] of <math>p_i</math> and <math>\delta(p_1,p_2)=\min(|\varphi_1-\varphi_2|,2\pi-|\varphi_1-\varphi_2|)</math> is the [[angular distance]] between the two points.
